exemplars.question: E1
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos makes this a powerful introduction by presenting Hannibal as the greatest general ever to fight Rome, while keeping his Roman readers on his side.
He begins with
Hannibal, Hamilcaris filius, Carthaginiensis
‘Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, a Carthaginian’
This bare list of name, father and nation, with no verb,
reads like an entry in a record. It introduces Hannibal at once through the father whose hatred he will inherit, and it ends on Carthaginiensis, the word that marks him out as Rome’s great enemy.
The opening is powerful because it is so confident: Nepos assumes the name alone is enough.
He then makes a bold claim:
non est infitiandum Hannibalem tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, quanto populus Romanus antecedat fortitudine cunctas nationes
‘it must not be denied that Hannibal surpassed the other generals in skill by as much as the Roman people surpass all nations in courage’
The litotes non est infitiandum
makes the praise sound reluctant but unavoidable, as if the facts force it out of Nepos,
and the balanced tanto … quanto comparison
sets Hannibal above every general exactly as high as Rome stands above every nation. Because Rome is flattered in the same breath, a Roman reader can accept this praise of an enemy.
Hannibal is raised to the level of Rome itself, which gives the introduction its force.
quotienscumque cum eo congressus est in Italia, semper discessit superior
‘as often as he fought with him in Italy, he always came away the winner’
The pairing of quotienscumque and semper
allows no exceptions, and the sentence ends on superior, so the last word we hear is his superiority.
Nepos goes further:
quod nisi domi civium suorum invidia debilitatus esset, Romanos videtur superare potuisse
‘if he had not been weakened at home by the jealousy of his own citizens, he seems to have been able to defeat the Romans’
This unreal condition
imagines Rome defeated, a shocking thought for a Roman reader, which the cautious videtur softens. It also blames Carthage, not Rome, for his failure,
so Hannibal becomes a tragic figure from the very first chapter.
The point is driven home in
multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem
‘the spite of many overcame the courage of one’
The antithesis of multorum and unius, and of obtrectatio and virtutem,

sums up his fate in one short, pointed sentence: one brave man against many petty ones. devicit is the language of the battlefield, so the only victory ever won over Hannibal is won by his own people.
Finally Nepos turns to his hatred of Rome:
velut hereditate relictum odium paternum erga Romanos
‘his father’s hatred of the Romans, left to him as if by inheritance’
The inheritance metaphor
makes this hatred part of who Hannibal is, handed down like property,
and
ut prius animam quam id deposuerit
‘that he laid down his life sooner than that hatred’
is hyperbole
showing how deep it runs.
The chapter ends
numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis
‘he never stopped waging war on the Romans in spirit’
numquam closes on an unbroken war,
so the introduction looks ahead to the whole Life and leaves the reader expecting a relentless enemy.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5). It engages closely with ‘powerful’ throughout, opening with a clear line of argument and linking most points back to it. A wide range of well-selected quotations covers the whole passage, each accurately translated. Features are precisely named and their effects are developed: the litotes makes the praise sound reluctant, the tanto … quanto comparison flatters Rome while raising Hannibal, and devicit is explained as a military word turned against his own people. The point on quotienscumque … semper is well observed but not linked back to the question, and the hyperbole could be developed further, which keeps this just short of full marks.

exemplars.question: E1
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos creates a powerful introduction by praising Hannibal very highly.
He starts with
Hannibal, Hamilcaris filius, Carthaginiensis
‘Hannibal, son of Hamilcar, a Carthaginian’
This is very short
and gets straight to the point, telling us who Hannibal is.
si verum est, quod nemo dubitat
‘if it is true, which no one doubts’
is a parenthesis
which reassures the Romans that they are the best before he praises Hannibal, so they will not be offended.
He then says
tanto praestitisse ceteros imperatores prudentia, quanto populus Romanus antecedat fortitudine cunctas nationes
‘he surpassed the other generals in wisdom as much as the Roman people surpass all nations in courage’
This is a comparison
which makes Hannibal seem as great as Rome,
which is a powerful way to introduce him.
Nepos then tells us that every time Hannibal fought the Romans in Italy he won, and that he would have beaten them if his own people had not been jealous of him.
multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem
‘the jealousy of many defeated the courage of one’
is an antithesis between many and one
which makes Hannibal seem like a lone hero.
velut hereditate relictum odium paternum
‘his father’s hatred, left as if by inheritance’
is a metaphor
showing that he got his hatred of Rome from his father.
numquam destiterit animo bellare cum Romanis
‘he never stopped fighting the Romans in his mind’
uses the strong word numquam for emphasis.
Overall Nepos makes this a powerful introduction because he shows Hannibal as a great general and a lifelong enemy of Rome.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4). It engages with the question, covers the whole passage, and quotes and translates sensibly throughout. The points on the parenthesis si verum est, quod nemo dubitat and on the antithesis of multorum and unius are well made. Elsewhere the development is thinner: the comparison is just called ‘a comparison’ with no mention of tanto … quanto, the opening is ‘very short’ without saying why that makes it powerful, and the point on numquam stops at ‘emphasis’. One paragraph retells the victories in Italy instead of analysing the Latin (quotienscumque … semper would have repaid attention). More precise naming of features, and fuller explanation of their effect, would lift this into Level 5.

exemplars.question: E1
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos makes this a powerful introduction because Hannibal is a great general.
He tells us that Hannibal was the son of Hamilcar and came from Carthage, and that he was better than all the other generals, just as the Romans were better than all other nations.
Nepos uses the word
imperatores
, which means
‘emperors’
, and this shows that Hannibal was very important.
Then Nepos says that Hannibal always won when he fought in Italy, but the people at home were jealous of him and that is why he lost.
There is
an antithesis
in
multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem
which is very effective.
odium
means ‘hatred’, and this shows Hannibal hated the Romans.
He hated them because his father did, and he kept on hating them all his life, even after he was driven out of his country.
This makes it a powerful introduction because we know he will be an important enemy of Rome.

exemplars.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2). There is some engagement with the question at the start and the end, but most of the answer retells the passage in English paraphrase. Only one Latin phrase is quoted; elsewhere single words are picked out (imperatores, odium), and imperatores is mistranslated as ‘emperors’ when here it means ‘generals’. The antithesis in multorum obtrectatio devicit unius virtutem is correctly spotted, but calling it ‘very effective’ is not development: the answer needs to say how setting the many against the one makes Hannibal’s fall seem unjust. Limited points, occasionally supported by the passage, place this in the middle of Level 2.

exemplars.question: E2c
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos makes the oath scene both vivid and solemn by letting Hannibal tell it himself, and by surrounding a small boy’s promise with the full weight of religion.
The story is told in direct speech:
pater meus inquit Hamilcar
‘my father Hamilcar,’ he said
Switching into Hannibal’s own words
makes the scene vivid, as if we are hearing a memory first-hand, and placing pater meus first frames the oath as a family matter, a debt owed to a father.
He then fixes the moment precisely:
puerulo me, utpote non amplius VIIII annos nato
‘when I was a little boy, being no more than nine years old’
The diminutive puerulo and the exact age
let us picture how small he was, which makes what follows all the more striking: a lifelong oath is laid on a child.
The setting is religious from the start:
Iovi optimo maximo hostias immolavit
‘he sacrificed victims to Jupiter Best and Greatest’
The full formal title of Jupiter, with its two superlatives,
sounds like the language of ritual itself and places the scene at an altar before the greatest of the gods.
quae divina res dum conficiebatur
‘while this sacred rite was being carried out’
keeps the sacrifice in front of us: everything that follows happens in the middle of it,
so the oath is sworn under the gods’ eyes, which makes it solemn.
Against this solemn background Nepos sets the boy’s excitement:
id cum libenter accepissem atque ab eo petere coepissem ne dubitaret ducere
‘when I had gladly accepted this and had begun to beg him not to hesitate to take me’
The eager libenter and the pleading petere coepissem
bring the boy to life, and his excitement about going on campaign contrasts sharply with the grave condition his father is about to set,
which makes the scene vivid and human.
Hamilcar’s reply is brief:
faciam, inquit, si mihi fidem, quam postulo, dederis
‘“I will,” he said, “if you give me the pledge that I demand”’
It opens with the single decisive word faciam, and the conditional
turns a father’s promise into a contract; postulo, ‘I demand’, is stern and formal.
The action follows at once:
simul me ad aram adduxit
‘at the same moment he led me to the altar’
simul quickens the pace, as if the boy has no time to think,
and
eamque ceteris remotis tenentem
‘holding it, with everyone else sent away’
adds a physical detail and a private setting:
we see the boy’s hands on the altar, alone with his father, so the moment feels both intimate and sacred.
Finally,
iurare iussit numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore
‘he ordered me to swear that I would never be on terms of friendship with the Romans’
The alliteration of iurare iussit
gives the command a ritual ring, and numquam makes the oath absolute and lifelong;
the scene ends on its most solemn words, an oath that will shape the rest of Hannibal’s life.

exemplars.commentary: This is an excellent response (Level 5, full marks). Both parts of the question are addressed throughout: vividness (the direct speech, the diminutive puerulo, the boy’s eagerness, the physical detail of holding the altar) and solemnity (the formal title of Jupiter, divina res, the stern postulo, the absolute numquam). Quotations are well selected from every part of the passage and accurately translated, and each feature is explained in terms of its effect as well as named. The contrast between the boy’s excitement and his father’s grave demand is a perceptive point that shows real engagement with the scene. Not every point needs to be this full to reach the top of the level, but the range and precision here are exemplary.

exemplars.question: E2c
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos makes the scene vivid by using direct speech.
pater meus inquit Hamilcar
‘my father Hamilcar,’ he said
is in direct speech, which makes it more vivid because we hear it from Hannibal himself.
Hannibal explains that when he was nine years old his father was going to Spain as a general and made a sacrifice to Jupiter before he left.
Iovi optimo maximo
‘to Jupiter best and greatest’
uses superlatives,
which makes it solemn.
libenter
means ‘gladly’ and shows that Hannibal really wanted to go with his father,
which makes him seem like a real child.
Hamilcar says
faciam, inquit, si mihi fidem, quam postulo, dederis
‘I will do it, he said, if you give me the faith which I ask for’
This is direct speech again, which makes it vivid, and it shows that Hamilcar is serious.
Then he took him to the altar, sent everyone else away, and made him hold the altar and swear.
numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore
‘that I would never be in friendship with the Romans’
uses numquam,
which shows how strong the oath was and that it would last for ever.
This makes the scene solemn because it is a very serious promise.

exemplars.commentary: This is a reasonable response (Level 3), towards the top of the level. It has a clear point about direct speech, made twice, and some development of the oath itself through numquam. However, it leans heavily on vividness and says little about how the scene is made solemn: the superlatives are called solemn without any explanation of why, and the religious language of divina res, the sacrifice and the altar would have given plenty to discuss. Two paragraphs simply narrate the story, and libenter is picked out as a single word. Translation is generally accurate. Some development and a selection of examples lead to tenable conclusions.

exemplars.question: E2c
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: In this passage Hannibal is telling the story of how his father Hamilcar took him to Spain when he was nine. Before they left, Hamilcar sacrificed to Jupiter and asked Hannibal if he wanted to come. Hannibal said yes and begged to go,
which is vivid.
aram
means ‘altar’, which is solemn because it is religious.
Hamilcar made him hold the altar and swear never to be friends with the Romans.
iurare
means ‘to swear’.
This oath is important because Hannibal kept it all his life and fought against Rome in many battles, like Cannae, and crossed the Alps with elephants.
So the scene is vivid and solemn because it is the start of Hannibal’s hatred of Rome.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very limited response (Level 1), at the top of the level. It understands the story and mentions both key words, but almost all of it is narrative paraphrase. The only Latin is two single words (aram, iurare); no phrase is quoted or analysed and no literary feature is identified. The third paragraph drifts away from the passage to Hannibal’s later career, which does not answer a question about this scene. ‘Vivid’ and ‘solemn’ are asserted, never shown. A start would be to quote and translate a whole phrase such as Iovi optimo maximo hostias immolavit and explain what the formal language adds.

exemplars.question: E4b
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos makes the crossing of the Alps seem heroic by stressing how great an obstacle the mountains were, by comparing Hannibal with Hercules, and by showing his relentless effort.
He builds up to the Alps:
saltum Pyrenaeum transiit
‘he crossed the Pyrenean pass’
This short, plain statement
makes crossing a whole mountain range sound routine, which prepares us for a far greater feat.
neminem nisi victum dimisit
‘he let no one go unless defeated’
is an emphatic negative
showing that nothing on the march could stop him,
so he arrives at the Alps already unbeaten.
The Alps themselves are a barrier between nations,
quae Italiam ab Gallia seiungunt
‘which separate Italy from Gaul’
, and
quas nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium transierat
‘which no one had ever crossed with an army before him except Hercules the Greek’
The strong negatives nemo umquam and the comparison with Hercules
put Hannibal in the company of a mythical hero: only a demigod had done this before,
which makes his achievement heroic in the literal sense.
quo facto is hodie saltus Graius appellatur
‘because of which that pass is today called the Graian pass’
reminds us that Hercules’ feat is still remembered in a place name, implying that Hannibal’s deserves the same lasting fame.
Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit
‘he cut down the Alpine tribesmen who tried to stop him crossing’
The violent verb concidit
shows him removing human obstacles as forcefully as natural ones.
Then
loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit
‘he opened up the ground, he built roads, he brought it about’
the asyndeton of three short verbs in the perfect
conveys relentless, practical labour, one achievement after another,
so the heroism lies in engineering as well as fighting.
ut ea elephantus ornatus ire posset, qua antea unus homo inermis vix poterat repere
‘that an equipped elephant could go along the route where before one unarmed man could scarcely crawl’
The contrast between the huge, laden elephant and one unarmed man, stressed by vix and repere,
measures how much he has changed the mountains.
hac copias traduxit in Italiamque pervenit
‘by this route he led his forces across and reached Italy’
is a short, calm ending: the goal is reached without fuss.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5), at the bottom of the level. It has a clear argument, covers the whole passage, and quotes accurately with good translations. The Hercules comparison is well developed, and the point about the place name is perceptive. The asyndeton of loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit is precisely analysed and linked to the question. Some later points are less fully linked to ‘heroic’: the striking contrast of the elephant and the man who could barely crawl is identified, but the answer does not draw out what it says about Hannibal, and the final point is brief. Those small gaps keep the mark at 13.

exemplars.question: E4b
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos presents the crossing of the Alps as a heroic achievement in several ways.
quas nemo umquam cum exercitu ante eum praeter Herculem Graium transierat
‘which no one had ever crossed with an army before him except Greek Hercules’
Nepos compares Hannibal to Hercules,
a great hero of mythology, so Hannibal seems like a hero too,
and the crossing seems almost superhuman because only Hercules had done it.
Alpicos conantes prohibere transitu concidit
‘he killed the Alpine people who were trying to stop him crossing’
shows that he had to fight as well as cross the mountains, which makes it harder and so more heroic.
loca patefecit, itinera muniit
‘he opened up places, he built roads’
is asyndeton
which makes it sound as if he did a lot of work quickly.
elephantus ornatus ire posset, qua antea unus homo inermis vix poterat repere
‘an equipped elephant could go where before one unarmed man could hardly crawl’
This is a contrast between the elephant and the man
which shows how difficult the route was before Hannibal changed it, and how much he achieved.
This is the most heroic part of the passage.

At the start of the passage Nepos tells us that Hannibal divided his army into three, sent one part to Africa, left one in Spain and took one to Italy, and that he crossed the Pyrenees and fought everyone on the way.
Overall the crossing seems heroic because it was so difficult.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4), at the top of the level. Its points are relevant and accurately supported: the Hercules comparison, the fighting with the Alpine tribes and the contrast of the elephant with the crawling man are all explained in terms of the question. The range is narrower than in the best answers, though: the opening of the passage is only narrated, so neminem nisi victum dimisit and the plain saltum Pyrenaeum transiit are missed, and the asyndeton is named with only a brief comment on speed. The answer also works out of order, which leaves the narrative tacked on at the end. Wider coverage and fuller analysis would take it into Level 5.

exemplars.question: E4b
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos makes the crossing of the Alps seem heroic because it was very difficult.
He tells us that Hannibal came to the Alps, which separate Italy from Gaul, and that no one had crossed them with an army before except Hercules.
This makes Hannibal seem as great as Hercules.
The Alpine tribes tried to stop him, but he killed them.
concidit
means
‘he fell’, which shows that the crossing was dangerous even for Hannibal.
There is
a tricolon
in
loca patefecit, itinera muniit, effecit
which emphasises what he did.
He made it possible for an elephant to go where before a man could barely crawl, and then he took his army into Italy.
This shows that the crossing was a heroic achievement.

exemplars.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the top of the level. It makes one sound point, that the comparison with Hercules makes Hannibal seem great, but makes it from English paraphrase instead of the Latin. Most of the answer narrates the passage. concidit is mistranslated as ‘he fell’ (here it is from concido, ‘cut down’), which leads to a point the passage does not support. The tricolon is correctly identified and quoted, but ‘emphasises what he did’ does not explain its effect. The excellent contrast of the elephant and the crawling man is mentioned only in English, with no analysis.

exemplars.question: E6
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos presents Hannibal as a master of cunning by showing him escape a trap through an ingenious trick, and then use deceit again and again to destroy Rome’s commanders.
hic clausus locorum angustiis noctu sine ullo detrimento exercitus se expedivit
‘trapped here by the narrowness of the terrain, he got himself out at night without any loss to his army’
The contrast between clausus near the start and se expedivit at the end
shows him turning an impossible position into an escape, and sine ullo detrimento stresses how complete it was.
Fabioque, callidissimo imperatori, dedit verba
‘and he tricked Fabius, a most cunning commander’
The superlative callidissimo

praises Fabius as the cleverest of generals in the very clause in which Hannibal fools him, so Hannibal seems cleverer still. The idiom dedit verba, literally ‘gave words’, is itself the language of trickery.
sarmenta in cornibus iuvencorum deligata incendit
‘he set fire to bundles of twigs tied to the horns of young bullocks’
The precise detail makes the trick vivid and shows how inventive it was.
quo repentino visu obiecto tantum terrorem iniecit exercitui Romanorum, ut egredi extra vallum nemo sit ausus
‘by presenting this sudden sight he struck such terror into the Roman army that no one dared to go outside the rampart’
The result clause, ending on nemo sit ausus,
shows a whole Roman army pinned down by a few burning cattle,
which shows the power of his cunning.
He uses the same skill against others:
dolo productum in proelium fugavit
‘having lured him into battle by a trick, he routed him’
, and Gracchus was killed
absens in insidias inductum
‘led into an ambush while Hannibal was absent’
absens suggests that his cunning works even at a distance.
pari modo interfecit
‘he killed him in the same way’
shows that ambush is his usual method.
nemo ei in acie restitit, nemo adversus eum post Cannensem pugnam in campo castra posuit
‘no one stood against him in battle, no one pitched camp against him in the open after the battle of Cannae’
The anaphora of nemo
emphasises that the Romans no longer dared to face him.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4), at the top of the level. It is well organised and focused on ‘cunning’, with a range of accurate quotations and translations from the whole passage. The analysis of callidissimo, praising Fabius just as he is fooled, is perceptive, and the point that a whole army is pinned down by the trick is well developed. The later points are thinner: absens and pari modo are noted briefly, and the titles of the Roman victims (magistrum equitum pari ac dictatorem imperio, quinquies consulem), which make each deception more impressive, are not discussed. The final point on the anaphora of nemo is not linked to cunning at all. With these developed, the answer would reach Level 5.

exemplars.question: E6
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos shows that Hannibal was very cunning.
Fabioque, callidissimo imperatori, dedit verba
‘he deceived Fabius, the cleverest general’
callidissimo is a superlative
which shows that Fabius was clever, but Hannibal was even cleverer because he tricked him.
Hannibal tied twigs to the horns of cattle, set them on fire, and let the cattle loose at night.
tantum terrorem iniecit exercitui Romanorum
‘he threw so much terror into the Roman army’
has alliteration of t
which emphasises the terror.
The Romans were too scared to leave their camp, which shows how well the trick worked.
dolo productum in proelium fugavit
‘he put him to flight, having led him into battle by a trick’
shows that he used tricks against Minucius as well.
He also killed Gracchus in an ambush and Marcellus in the same way.
This shows that Hannibal was a master of cunning because he beat many Roman generals with tricks.

exemplars.commentary: This is a reasonable response (Level 3), at the top of the level. It stays focused on cunning and makes two good points: callidissimo makes Hannibal’s deception of Fabius more impressive, and dolo productum shows deceit used again. Translations are sound. Elsewhere the development is limited: the trick with the cattle is narrated, the alliteration point stops at ‘emphasises’, and the deaths of Gracchus and Marcellus are told in English when absens and pari modo offered clear evidence of cunning. The answer is also short, and the end of the passage is not used. More points, each fully developed, would move it into Level 4.

exemplars.question: E6
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: In this passage Hannibal is trapped but he escapes at night.
Fabius was a Roman general who was called the Delayer because he refused to fight Hannibal in a pitched battle, and in the end his tactics worked.
Hannibal used cattle with fire on their horns to scare the Romans. Then he beat Minucius and killed Gracchus and Marcellus.
insidias
means ‘ambush’.
Hannibal was a great general because he never lost a battle in Italy, and nobody dared to fight him after Cannae.
So he was very cunning.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very limited response (Level 1). It shows a general understanding of what happens, but no Latin is quoted beyond the single word insidias, and no literary feature is identified. The material on Fabius’ tactics comes from outside the passage and does not answer the question. The last paragraph is about Hannibal’s success in general and has nothing to do with cunning, and the link to the question is only asserted in the final sentence. To improve, the answer needed to quote and translate phrases such as dedit verba or dolo productum and explain how they show deceit.

exemplars.question: E11
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos makes the story entertaining by setting up a contest of wits between the cleverest of men and the greedy Cretans, letting the reader in on the trick, and ending with a comic reversal.
vidit autem vir omnium callidissimus
‘but this man, the cleverest of all, saw’
The superlative, strengthened by omnium,
announces Hannibal as a trickster before we know what he will do, so we read on expecting something clever.
Against him stand the Cretans:
propter avaritiam Cretensium
‘because of the greed of the Cretans’
Defining them by their greed makes them deserve what is coming,
so the reader can enjoy seeing them fooled.
itaque capit tale consilium
‘so he forms the following plan’
This short sentence in the historic present, with tale pointing forward,
builds anticipation, like a storyteller pausing before the trick.
amphoras complures complet plumbo, summas operit auro et argento
‘he fills several jars with lead and covers the tops with gold and silver’
The asyndeton and the historic presents

make the preparations quick and concrete, and the alliteration of complures complet gives a playful sound. The contrast between cheap lead below and gold and silver on top is the whole joke in miniature.
has praesentibus principibus deponit in templo Dianae
‘he deposits these in the temple of Diana in the presence of the leading men’
The alliteration of p
draws attention to the solemn audience, and the temple setting makes it funnier: the leading citizens are formally witnessing a sham.
simulans se suas fortunas illorum fidei credere
‘pretending that he was entrusting his fortune to their good faith’
simulans lets us in on the pretence, and fidei is ironic, since it is the Cretans’ lack of good faith that he fears.
We share the joke with Hannibal, which is what makes the story entertaining.
Meanwhile
statuas aeneas … omni sua pecunia complet easque in propatulo domi abicit
‘he fills bronze statues with all his money and throws them down in the open courtyard of his house’
abicit, ‘throws down’,
makes the real treasure seem carelessly tossed aside, an audacious bluff.
Gortynii templum magna cura custodiunt non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale
‘the people of Gortyn guard the temple with great care, not so much against others as against Hannibal’
The non tam … quam construction
delivers the punchline: they guard lead against the very man who left it,
ne ille inscientibus iis tolleret sua
‘in case he took away his own property without their knowledge’
while his money lies in full view.
The comic reversal makes the greedy Cretans look foolish and gives the story its entertaining ending.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5). It shows a clear grasp of what makes the episode entertaining (the contest of wits, the reader’s share in the secret, the reversal) and builds the answer around it. Quotation is plentiful and accurate, covering the passage from the first line to the last, and features are explained precisely: the storyteller’s pause in capit tale consilium, the irony of fidei, and the punchline of non tam … quam. The statues are linked to the bluff but not back to the question, and the alliteration points are light, but this is a convincing and well-supported answer.

exemplars.question: E11
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: The story is entertaining because Hannibal tricks the Cretans.
Hannibal was worried because he had a lot of money and the Cretans were greedy, so he made a plan.
amphoras complures complet plumbo
‘he fills many jars with lead’
is in the historic present,
which makes it more vivid and exciting.
He put gold and silver on top and left the jars in the temple of Diana in front of the leading men.
simulans se suas fortunas illorum fidei credere
‘pretending that he trusted his fortune to their faith’
shows that he is lying to them, which is funny.
He put his real money in bronze statues and left them at his house.
custodiunt
means
‘they keep it for themselves’, which shows the Cretans were greedy.
This is entertaining because the Cretans think they have Hannibal’s money but they only have lead.

exemplars.commentary: This is a reasonable response (Level 3), at the bottom of the level. It understands the trick and makes some relevant points: the historic present is identified, and simulans is rightly seen as showing deception. Much of the answer narrates, though, the points are brief, and custodiunt is misunderstood as the Cretans keeping the money for themselves, when Nepos says they guard the temple against Hannibal. That misreading means the answer misses the comic reversal of non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale, which is the heart of the entertainment. The conclusion is tenable but rests on paraphrase.

exemplars.question: E11
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Hannibal went to Crete with a lot of money. He knew the Cretans were greedy so he thought of a clever plan. He filled jars with lead, put gold and silver on top and left them in the temple. Then he hid his real money in statues.
callidissimus
is a superlative.
Hannibal was clever in many other places too, for example when he tricked Fabius with the cattle.
The Cretans guarded the temple so that Hannibal would not take his money back.
This is entertaining because it is a clever trick.

exemplars.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the bottom of the level. It tells the story accurately, but almost entirely in English paraphrase. The only Latin is the single word callidissimus, labelled a superlative with no comment on its effect. The trick on Fabius comes from elsewhere in the Life and does not help with a question about this passage. The answer never explains why the trick is entertaining: the reader’s knowledge of the pretence (simulans) and the irony of the Cretans guarding lead were there to be discussed.

exemplars.question: E16b
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos makes Hannibal’s last moments dramatic by slowly closing a trap around him, showing the danger through the eyes of a boy, and ending on Hannibal’s calm choice of death.
huc cum legati Romanorum venissent ac multitudine domum eius circumdedissent
‘when the Roman envoys had come here and had surrounded his house with a large force’
The two pluperfect verbs
tell us that the trap is already set before the scene begins, so the reader knows more than Hannibal does,
which creates dramatic irony and tension.
puer ab ianua prospiciens Hannibali dixit plures praeter consuetudinem armatos apparere
‘a boy looking out from the door told Hannibal that more armed men than usual were appearing’
Seeing the danger through the eyes of a boy
makes the scene immediate, and praeter consuetudinem quietly signals that something is wrong.
ut omnes fores aedificii circumiret ac propere sibi nuntiaret, num eodem modo undique obsideretur
‘to go round all the doors of the building and quickly report to him whether he was being besieged on every side in the same way’
The urgent propere and the indirect question
keep us waiting with Hannibal for the answer,
and the reply comes fast:
puer cum celeriter, quid esset, renuntiasset omnesque exitus occupatos ostendisset
‘when the boy had quickly reported what was happening and shown that all the exits were occupied’
celeriter, echoing propere,
speeds up the narrative, and omnes exitus occupatos closes every escape at once.
sensit id non fortuito factum, sed se peti
‘he realised that this had not happened by chance, but that he was the target’
The antithesis of non fortuito and se peti
marks the moment of realisation,
the turning point of the drama.
neque sibi diutius vitam esse retinendam
‘and that he must not keep his life any longer’
follows at once, without hesitation.
quam ne alieno arbitrio dimitteret, memor pristinarum virtutum
‘so as not to give it up at another’s will, remembering his former courage’
He chooses to keep control of his fate, which makes the death dignified,
and
the sentence holds back its main verb to the very end:
venenum, quod semper secum habere consuerat, sumpsit
‘he took the poison which he had always been in the habit of keeping with him’
sumpsit is the last word of the scene, so the drama ends on his final act.

exemplars.commentary: This is a very good response (Level 5), at the bottom of the level. It is carefully structured around the build-up of tension, and the observation that the pluperfects let the reader know about the trap before Hannibal does is perceptive. Quotations are accurate and well chosen from the whole passage, and the pairing of propere and celeriter is a neat point about pace. The final paragraph is strong on the placing of sumpsit, though semper (he had carried the poison all along) could have been developed. A few points stop at the effect without returning to ‘dramatic’, which keeps the mark at 13.

exemplars.question: E16b
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: Nepos makes Hannibal’s last moments dramatic in several ways.
multitudine domum eius circumdedissent
‘they had surrounded his house with a crowd’
This shows that the Romans had sent a lot of men, which makes the situation dangerous, and it is dramatic because Hannibal is trapped.
plures praeter consuetudinem armatos apparere
‘more armed men than usual were appearing’
builds tension because it shows that something unusual is happening.
Hannibal told the boy to go round all the doors and find out if the house was surrounded.
propere
means ‘quickly’
and shows he is in a hurry.
omnesque exitus occupatos
‘and all the exits were occupied’
shows that there is no escape, which is dramatic.
sensit id non fortuito factum, sed se peti
‘he realised this had not happened by chance, but that he was being sought’
This is an antithesis
which shows the moment when Hannibal realises what is happening.
memor pristinarum virtutum
‘remembering his former virtues’
shows that he wants to die bravely.
venenum, quod semper secum habere consuerat, sumpsit
‘he took the poison which he always kept with him’
The passage ends with his death, which is very dramatic.

exemplars.commentary: This is a good response (Level 4), at the bottom of the level. It works through the whole passage with relevant, accurately translated quotations and keeps the focus on drama: the sense of being trapped, the unusual number of armed men, the moment of realisation. The development is sound but uneven: the antithesis is named and only briefly explained, propere is quoted as a single word, and the last sentence asserts that the ending is dramatic without showing how Nepos makes it so (the delay of sumpsit, the significance of semper). Fewer, more fully developed points would serve it better.

exemplars.question: E16b
exemplars.source: Practice answer written for Classicalia and marked against OCR’s level descriptors

segments.t: The Romans came to Hannibal’s house and surrounded it. A boy saw them and told Hannibal there were lots of armed men. Hannibal told him to check all the doors and the boy came back and said all the exits were blocked.
This is dramatic because Hannibal is trapped.
sensit id non fortuito factum
‘he felt that this was not done by luck’
shows that Hannibal realised what was happening.
neque sibi diutius vitam esse retinendam
‘and that his life would not be held for long’
shows that he knew he was going to be killed.
There is
a lot of suspense
in this passage,
which makes it dramatic.
In the end Hannibal took poison and died.
This is a dramatic ending to his life.

exemplars.commentary: This is a limited response (Level 2), at the top of the level. There is clear engagement with ‘dramatic’ and the idea of a trap, and two phrases are quoted. However, the gerundive in neque sibi diutius vitam esse retinendam is mistranslated: Nepos says Hannibal decided he must no longer keep his life, which is his own choice, not that he expected to be killed. That misreading hides the most important point about the ending. ‘Suspense’ is mentioned without any example of how it is created, and much of the answer narrates. Points such as the boy’s view from the door or the delay of sumpsit to the end of the sentence would have raised the level.

drills.question: E5
drills.latin: utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit, Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares
drills.weak: Nepos uses the word occidit (‘killed’), which shows that Hannibal was violent.
drills.strong: utriusque exercitus uno proelio fugavit, Paulum consulem occidit et aliquot praeterea consulares (‘he routed the armies of both in a single battle, and killed the consul Paulus and several ex-consuls besides’): uno proelio set against utriusque exercitus makes Cannae one crushing blow, the asyndeton of fugavit and occidit piles up the results, and the ranks of the dead, a consul and several ex-consuls, show how much of Rome’s leadership fell at once, so the victories seem overwhelming.
drills.why: A single word with an obvious meaning shows nothing about Nepos’ writing. Quoting the whole phrase brings in uno proelio and the ranks of the dead, which is where the overwhelming effect lies.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 4: In this passage, how does Nepos make Hannibal’s victories in Italy seem overwhelming?

drills.question: E15
drills.latin: postquam autem naves suas oppletas conspexerunt serpentibus, nova re perterriti
drills.strong: postquam autem naves suas oppletas conspexerunt serpentibus, nova re perterriti (‘but after they saw their ships filled with snakes, utterly terrified by this new thing’): serpentibus is held back to the end of its clause, so the reader discovers the snakes at the same moment as the sailors, and the strong compound perterriti marks the sudden switch from laughter to panic, which makes the moment dramatic.
drills.why: Knowing what one word means is not analysis. The drama comes from where Nepos puts the word and what it does to the sailors.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 11: In this passage, how does Nepos make the defeat of the Pergamene fleet dramatic?

drills.question: E7b
drills.latin: pulsus incredibile dictu biduo et duabus noctibus Hadrumetum pervenit
drills.weak: After losing at Zama, Hannibal travelled to Hadrumetum in two days and two nights, which was three hundred miles away. Then the Numidians ambushed him but he beat them.
drills.strong: pulsus incredibile dictu biduo et duabus noctibus Hadrumetum pervenit (‘beaten, incredible to say, he reached Hadrumetum in two days and two nights’): the single participle pulsus disposes of the defeat in one word, Nepos’ aside incredibile dictu shares his own amazement with the reader, and the precise biduo et duabus noctibus makes the speed concrete, so the narrative races on as fast as Hannibal does.
drills.why: Retelling what happens gains no credit by itself. The stronger version picks out how Nepos tells it: the brevity, the aside and the precise detail.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 6: In this passage, how does Nepos make this passage fast-moving and vivid?

drills.question: E9
drills.latin: bona eius publicarunt, domum a fundamentis disiecerunt, ipsum exulem iudicarunt
drills.weak: The Carthaginians sent two ships after him, took his property, knocked down his house and made him an exile.
drills.strong: bona eius publicarunt, domum a fundamentis disiecerunt, ipsum exulem iudicarunt (‘they confiscated his property, tore his house down from its foundations, and declared him an exile’): the asyndetic tricolon, each clause ending on a perfect verb, makes the punishments fall one after another; a fundamentis shows a spite that goes beyond justice, and the climax on ipsum exulem turns from his possessions to the man himself, which seems all the more unjust after his careful service to the treasury.
drills.why: The weak point is an accurate summary, and that is all it is. The stronger version shows how the shape of the sentence makes the punishment seem excessive.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 7: In this passage, how does Nepos make Hannibal’s fall from power in Carthage seem unjust?

drills.question: E14
drills.latin: Hannibal, ut palam faceret suis, quo loco Eumenes esset, tabellarium in scapha cum caduceo mittit
drills.weak: Hannibal sent a messenger in a boat to find out where Eumenes was.
drills.strong: Hannibal, ut palam faceret suis, quo loco Eumenes esset, tabellarium in scapha cum caduceo mittit (‘to make clear to his men where Eumenes was, Hannibal sends a messenger in a small boat with a herald’s staff’): the vivid historic present mittit and the details of the little boat and the herald’s staff, the sign of a peace envoy, let us see the disguise; the purpose clause tells us the real aim first, so we watch the enemy trust the messenger knowing what he is for, which makes the trick entertaining.
drills.why: Narrative tells the reader what happened; the question asks how Nepos makes it entertaining. Here the answer is that he lets us into the secret before the enemy.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 11: In this passage, how does Nepos make Hannibal’s trick with the messenger entertaining for the reader?

drills.question: E14
drills.latin: statim ad Eumenem deductus est, quod nemo dubitabat, quin aliquid de pace esset scriptum
drills.weak: statim ad Eumenem deductus est uses the word statim, which emphasises it.
drills.strong: statim ad Eumenem deductus est, quod nemo dubitabat, quin aliquid de pace esset scriptum (‘he was immediately taken to Eumenes, because no one doubted that something about peace had been written’): statim shows how easily the enemy is fooled, and the irony of nemo dubitabat entertains the reader, who knows the letter holds only insults while everyone on Eumenes’ side takes it for a peace offer.
drills.why: ‘Emphasises it’ explains nothing. Say what is emphasised and why that matters to the question.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 11: In this passage, how does Nepos make Hannibal’s trick with the messenger entertaining for the reader?

drills.question: E5
drills.latin: qua valetudine cum etiam tum premeretur lecticaque ferretur, C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit
drills.weak: Nepos uses a cum clause here to show that Hannibal was ill.
drills.strong: qua valetudine cum etiam tum premeretur lecticaque ferretur, C. Flaminium consulem apud Trasumenum cum exercitu insidiis circumventum occidit (‘while he was still weighed down by this illness and being carried in a litter, he trapped the consul Gaius Flaminius and his army in an ambush at Trasimene and killed him’): the cum clause shows Hannibal at his weakest, half-blind and carried in a litter, and sets this against the destruction of a consul and his whole army, so even sick he cannot be beaten, and the victories seem overwhelming.
drills.why: Naming the grammar is not the same as analysing it. The point is what the illness adds to the victory.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 4: In this passage, how does Nepos make Hannibal’s victories in Italy seem overwhelming?

drills.question: E17
drills.latin: sic vir fortissimus, multis variisque perfunctus laboribus, anno acquievit septuagesimo
drills.weak: vir fortissimus is a superlative, which emphasises how brave he was.
drills.strong: sic vir fortissimus, multis variisque perfunctus laboribus, anno acquievit septuagesimo (‘so this bravest of men, having come through many and varied labours, found rest in his seventieth year’): the superlative fortissimus gives Nepos’ final verdict, multis variisque … laboribus recalls the whole life the reader has just followed, and acquievit, ‘found rest’, is a gentle word for a death by poison, so the Life closes on peace after struggle, a fitting end for a hero.
drills.why: The weak point names the superlative and repeats its meaning. The stronger version sets it in the whole sentence and links it to ‘fitting close’.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 12–13: In this passage, how does Nepos bring the Life of Hannibal to a fitting close?

drills.question: E14
drills.latin: at Eumenes soluta epistula nihil in ea repperit, nisi quae ad irridendum eum pertinerent
drills.weak: Eumenes was the king of Pergamum, which was an ally of Rome, and this is why Hannibal was fighting him.
drills.strong: at Eumenes soluta epistula nihil in ea repperit, nisi quae ad irridendum eum pertinerent (‘but when Eumenes opened the letter he found nothing in it except things meant to mock him’): the king, expecting a peace offer, finds only insults; nihil … nisi and ad irridendum make mockery the letter’s whole purpose, and after nemo dubitabat the let-down is all the funnier, which is what makes the trick entertaining.
drills.why: Background about Pergamum may be true, but it does not answer how Nepos makes the trick entertaining. Every point should be about the passage and the question’s key word.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 11: In this passage, how does Nepos make Hannibal’s trick with the messenger entertaining for the reader?

drills.question: E9
drills.latin: in eo magistratu pari diligentia se Hannibal praebuit, ac fuerat in bello
drills.weak: Hannibal was a brilliant general who crossed the Alps and won at Cannae, so it is unjust that he was exiled.
drills.strong: in eo magistratu pari diligentia se Hannibal praebuit, ac fuerat in bello (‘in that office Hannibal showed the same diligence as he had in war’): Nepos stresses that he served Carthage just as well in peace, and the non solum … sed etiam that follows shows him paying Rome and still leaving a surplus, so when his own city confiscates his property and destroys his house, the punishment seems shockingly unjust.
drills.why: The Alps and Cannae are not in this passage. The passage gives its own evidence of his service to Carthage, and the point should come from that.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 7: In this passage, how does Nepos make Hannibal’s fall from power in Carthage seem unjust?

drills.question: E15
drills.latin: quae iacta initio risum pugnantibus concitarunt
drills.weak: quae iacta initio risum pugnantibus concitarunt means ‘which, thrown at the start, made the fighters run’, so they were scared at once.
drills.strong: quae iacta initio risum pugnantibus concitarunt (‘when these were thrown, at first they made the fighting men laugh’): risum is laughter, and initio marks it as only the first reaction; the Pergamenes’ amusement at a few clay pots sets up the drama, because moments later the laughter turns to terror when the snakes appear.
drills.why: risum (laughter) was taken for a verb of running. The misreading reverses the point: the drama comes from the change from laughter to panic.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 11: In this passage, how does Nepos make the defeat of the Pergamene fleet dramatic?

drills.question: E7b
drills.latin: quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit
drills.weak: quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit means ‘he not only fled from them but was also oppressed by them’, which shows how much he suffered.
drills.strong: quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit (‘he not only escaped them but even overpowered them’): oppressit is active, with Hannibal as its subject and ipsos as its object; non solum … sed etiam builds to a climax, so even an ambush during a retreat ends in his victory, which keeps the passage fast-moving and vivid.
drills.why: oppressit is an active verb: Hannibal does the overpowering. Getting the voice wrong turns his triumph into suffering.
drills.context: Nepos, Hannibal 6: In this passage, how does Nepos make this passage fast-moving and vivid?

comments.text: Centres have become more aware of the need for developed analysis in 15-mark response questions: quoting a meaningful portion of Latin, then translating and discussing it in order to answer the question.
For 15-mark questions, candidates should be encouraged to quote and translate whole Latin phrases.
In some rare cases, the entire response was limited by having no reference at all to the Latin texts.
Fragmentary approaches which zone in on isolated words are unlikely to be credited.
focused too much on single isolated words, or words with English translations of Latin words which were easily recognisable (e.g. equus Troianus)
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025 (candidates who did less well)

comments.text: produced undeveloped analysis in 15-mark responses, often retelling the narrative with English paraphrases, or picking out isolated words with obvious English derivations but which did not show knowledge of their context in the passage
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024 (candidates who did less well)

comments.text: The most successful responses were able to capture the drama in this scene rather than simply narrating what happened in a linear progression through the passage.

While many scripts were extremely impressive, it was noticeable that a sizeable number were very narrative-heavy in their approaches. These responses tended to repeat the narrative of the text with some analysis of particular word choices but often neglecting the rich literary features that the texts contained.
In some cases, there was also a tendency to simply go through the narration of the passage to show how interesting it was. Greater levels of (stylistic) analysis would help prevent this shortcoming.
produced insightful responses to 15-mark questions by providing relevant evidence from the Latin texts and detailed discussion of relevant literary devices
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024 (candidates who did well)

comments.text: contained detailed discussion of relevant literary devices, both identifying these features and explaining their effects well
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025 (candidates who did well)

comments.text: Literary features can then be further analysed, and their relevance carefully explained.
Knowledge of the style of authors was also in evidence, though at times the development of these points could be stronger in order to point out the effects of such devices.
did not appreciate or evaluate the wealth of literary and rhetorical devices
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2025 (candidates who did less well)

comments.text: Several candidates seemed to find the use of litotes at times when an author made a negation. It should be noted that litotes is a literary device in which an author uses an understatement (often through mentioning the negative of a positive quality) which has the effect of adding an ironic tone or downplaying some fact.
Candidates were able to identify a range of emotions from outrage to sorrow and indignation, all of which were explained with well-selected evidence.
15-mark responses were focused on the question being asked, e.g. how the passage is ‘dramatic’, etc.
comments.source: OCR examiners’ report, H443/03 June 2024 (candidates who did well)

comments.text: Both content and use of language should be linked to the original question – e.g. how is a passage lively, or vivid, or how does it show an impressive character?
A piece of literary style is identified and discussed, before the whole point is clearly linked back to the question.

A range of points should be taken from the whole passage: sometimes, candidates offer perhaps multiple points of analysis on the same Latin quote which restricts the attention they give to other parts of the passage.

As often happens, a few candidates spent too much time on the 15-mark questions and ended up having to finish the 20-mark essay abruptly. The importance of good timing should be noted again by all centres.
It is always worth asking: are candidates spending too much time on the 15-mark questions?
There is ample quotation of Latin which is embedded in the context of the overall narrative.
